newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania, seeking IMF loans, posts record inflation.
newsitem.headline: Romania, seeking IMF loans, posts record inflation.

text.p: Romania said on Wednesday that its inflation rate hit a monthly record of more than 30 percent for March, far in excess of expectations, as the government signed a letter of intent to restore suspended Western credits.

The head of an IMF delegation monitoring the country's progress in reforms ahead of the Fund's board meeting on the credits this month praised a government programme. But he said he wanted evidence structural changes were being tackled.

On the eve of presenting an austerity budget to parliament, the government said it was closing two of Romania's 11 largely idle oil refineries and the Central Bank said it was withdrawing licences from two debt-ridden banks, the first such instances since the 1989 fall of communism.

Government inflation figures for March of 30.7 percent, the highest in the post-communist era, shocked bankers two days after Central Bank (BNR) forecasts had suggested the figure was no more than 12 percent.
February's inflation of 18.8 percent, a 45-month high, included the first price rises for staples and utilities in the reform programme and their effect clearly reverberated into March.
"I hope the IMF will not be scared off by this figure, especially considering it includes serveral price adjustments," Central Bank spokesman Adrian Vasilescu said by telephone.
"We might have another inflation blip in May after price rises in thermal power. But afterwards we will probably be the only country in eastern Europe to be rid of adjustments."

Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara and Central Bank chief Mugur Isarescu signed the letter of intent, viewed as a signal to attract overdue Western investment, and turned it over to the IMF's chief negotiator for Romania.
Neither side disclosed the letter's contents. Government sources say Romania is seeking about $400 million in credits from the IMF and up to $600 million from the World Bank.
IMF negotiator Poul Thomsen, speaking before the inflation figure was announced, said the government's reform programme, drawn up in February, was proceeding well.
"I'm encouraged in many respects by the main stabilisation achieved by the government," he told reporters.
"We are pleased that the programme is on track and in some areas is doing better than (planned). Previous programmes have collapsed in months because of the lack of structural reforms."

But he hoped measures to restructure or close inefficient industries and farms "will be put in place within weeks". He also said approval of the government's tough budget was vital to the programme's success.
Before the IMF's arrival, the government rushed to approve a long-awaited bill on bank privatisation, due to be debated by parliament starting next week.
The Central Bank has tightened monetary policy to restore confidence in the leu currency after removing restrictions on foreign exchange markets.

The 1997 budget calls for monthly inflation to be reduced to 2.2 percent by the end of the year. The budget deficit, three times over target last year at 5.8 percent of gross domestic product, is to be pared to 4.5 percent this year.
The IMF halted credits to Romania last year after the leftist government, thrown out of office by centrists last November, overshot spending targets and slapped curbs on foreign exchange markets.

Many Romanian and Western economists have said slow reforms and overspending by the ex-communists destabilised the economy and sent Romanian living standards plunging below those of other east European countries.
